newsitem.title: USA: INSTANT VIEW - US March int'l trade gap $8.51 bln.
newsitem.headline: INSTANT VIEW - US March int'l trade gap $8.51 bln.

text.p: Following are comments from U.S. economists after the Commerce Department reported the international trade gap fell to $8.51 in March compared to an upwardly revised $10.54 billion gap in February.
U.S. economists in a Reuters survey had expected a $10.3 billion trade deficit in March.
WAYNE AYERS, CHIEF ECONOMIST, BANK OF BOSTON: "I don't think it's really scewed. The extraordinary performance of exports really tells the story."

Speaking on Reuters Financial Television, Ayers said he expected the dollar "to weaken a bit vis-a-vis the yen," but noted overall that "the headline number this morning was eclipsed by the headline number of yesterday of the (Federal Reserve's) inaction."

KATHLEEN STEPHANSEN, SENIOR ECONOMIST, DONALDSON, LUFKIN AND JENRETTE SECURITIES CORP: "Obviously, it's a sharper contraction than anticipated. This will, all else being equal, prompt an upward revision of first quarter GDP (Gross Domestic Product) growth."

RON LEVEN, GLOBAL CURRENCY STRATEGIST, J.P. MORGAN & CO INC: "On the surface it's a good number. The overall deficit was much lower than the market was looking for. It's going to force us to push up our GDP growth forecast.
"There's a lot of of volatility in these numbers on a month-to-month basis. It is, on the balance, constructive."
CARY LEAHEY, SENIOR FINANCIAL MARKETS ECONOMIST, LEHMAN GOVERNMENT SECURITIES INC: "With exports up 4.1 percent, maybe $1.0 billion of (that) was due to the $1.0 billion extra in aircraft.

"This is an unfriendly number for the market because it adds probably another 1/4 to 1/3 of a percent to GDP growth almost guaranteeing a 6.0 percent number in the first quarter. But it may be helpful to the dollar," Leahey added.

GARY THAYER, SENIOR ECONOMIST, A.G. EDWARDS & SONS: "It's good news for the dollar. There have been a couple of reports lately, particularly the Japanese trade surplus widening, which had people concerned that our trade deficit would also widen. Maybe it will in the next a couple of months, but today's numbers show (there's no) immediate problem.

"I don't think this is going to be a trend going forward," Thayer added. "I think the dollar is still strong. I think our policy on the dollar is still to have a strong dollar. Although the dollar has come off a fair amount against the yen, it's still very high against many other currencies."

KEVIN LOGAN, SENIOR MARKET ECONOMIST, DRESDNER KLEINWORT BENSON NORTH AMERICA LLC: "We had a big jump in exports. We thought they would go up, but it was more than we thought. We had strong production in March and it seems that some of it was going into the export market.

"It very much looks like GDP will be revised higher on the basis of this (data). If nothing else changes, this would lift the (first quarter) GDP estimate up 0.7 percent from 5.6 percent to 6.3 percent."

JOHN ROTHFIELD, INTERNATIONAL ECONOMIST, NATIONSBANC-CRT: "There are some special factors. Lumpy items such as aircraft exports were higher, but it seems as though the pickup in the Canadian economy may be starting to reduce their trade surplus with the U.S. and as far as Western Europe goes we're seeing some evidence there as well.

"Also from the (purchasing managers) survey, export orders late in the first quarter were looking pretty good as well. This is encouraging for the dollar in the sense that U.S. export growth in real terms looks like it will remain at about 8.0 percent per annum this year," he added.
